---
title: "Tracing & diagnostics"
description: "Turn on the trace, read what the library actually did, and check a game before you even launch it."
---

Games rarely tell you *why* multiplayer didn't come up. EOS Reimagined ships its own diagnostics
so you don't have to guess: a structured **trace** the library writes itself, an ordinary **EOS
log** channel for developers, and an **import census tool** that predicts whether a game can load
the library at all.

## The trace

The trace is a versioned [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) stream written by the library —
independent of the game, which never has to cooperate. It is **off by default**, and off means
*off*: no run directory, no files, nothing on disk.

Turn it on with one variable (or the [`trace_level`](configuration.qmd) key):

```sh
EOSR_TRACE=lifecycle ./the-game
```

| Level | What you get |
|---|---|
| `off` | Nothing (default). No files are created. |
| `errors` | Failed calls and callbacks, dropped connections, config diagnostics. |
| `lifecycle` | The above, plus async call/callback pairs, notifications, and every network lifecycle event: discover, handshake, adopt, drop, search, P2P open/close. **The level to start with.** |
| `full` | Every EOS call and return, for every function. Verbose; for pinning down a specific interaction. |

Each level is a strict superset of the one below, so raising it only adds records.

### Where it goes

Each run gets its own directory under `<data-dir>/traces/` (configurable via `trace_dir`), named
like `run-20260713T004500Z-48213-a1` — timestamp, PID, and a collision suffix, so simultaneous
instances never fight over a directory:

```
~/.local/share/eos-reimagined/traces/run-20260713T004500Z-48213-a1/
├── runtime.json      # written once at startup: build, OS, run id, resolved config
├── trace.jsonl       # the live event stream
└── trace.1.jsonl …   # rotated files, newest first
```

Rotation is bounded and hard: a file is capped at `trace_max_bytes` (default 64 MiB), at most
`trace_max_rotated_files` (default 8) rotated files are kept, and no file ever exceeds the cap.
A killed process costs at most the one torn final line.

### What a record looks like

One JSON object per line, each with a shared envelope (sequence number, monotonic timestamp,
PID, logical thread label, kind) and a kind-specific body:

```json
{"v":1,"seq":41,"t":8123456789,"pid":48213,"inst":"alice","tid":"t#0",
 "kind":"call","fn":"EOS_Connect_Login","api":2,"corr":7,"args":{...}}
```

An async call mints a correlation ID that its return *and* its later callback carry, so you can
stitch a request to its completion across the ticks between them. Handles and player IDs never
appear raw — each object gets a stable local label (`session#3`, `puid#7`), and peer lifecycle
records carry a truncated, domain-separated **fingerprint** that lets two machines' traces be
joined on a peer without either file containing a real ID.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Safe to share, by construction

At no level does the trace contain private keys, credentials or tokens, message payloads (lengths
and metadata only), raw account IDs, or free text. The one caveat: `runtime.json` echoes your
display name and `instance_label` — fine on your own disk, worth a glance before posting a whole
run directory to a public issue.
:::

### Config problems land here too

Every rejected, clamped, or ignored [configuration](configuration.qmd) value becomes a
`meta`/`config` record with stable field/source/reason codes — so "why is my setting ignored?"
is answered by the first screenful of `trace.jsonl`. (With tracing off, those diagnostics go
best-effort to the EOS log callback instead; the library never creates files just to complain.)

Failure is engineered to be boring: if a write fails mid-run (disk full, permissions), the sink
disables itself, says so once through the logger, and the game never notices.

### `EOSR_RUN_DIR`: bring your own run directory

Test harnesses that launch the game themselves can set `EOSR_RUN_DIR` to a directory they
already created; the library then writes only its own files (`runtime.json`, `trace.jsonl`)
into it and never creates the directory itself. Most people never need this — it exists so
automated alpha runs own the whole run folder.

## The EOS log channel

Separate from the trace, the library implements the SDK's own logging surface:
`EOS_Logging_SetCallback` and `EOS_Logging_SetLogLevel` work, and the
[`log_level`](configuration.qmd) key sets the initial threshold (default `off` for players;
the callback default is Warning once a game installs one). Messages go **only to the game's
callback** — there is no log file. If you're not the game's developer, use the trace instead.

## `inspect_game.py`: will this game even load?

A game resolves every EOS symbol it imports *when the library loads* — or, for a Unity/Mono
title, on the first P/Invoke into it. One missing symbol kills the process before a single line
of the SDK runs, usually without a word of explanation. Current builds export the **complete**
EOS surface precisely to retire that failure class, but the census is still the first thing to
run on a new game: it shows exactly *which EOS families the game touches*, so you can read it
against the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd) and predict whether the parts it leans on actually function —
and it catches you when an older artifact is still in the game folder.

[`tools/inspect_game.py`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/blob/main/tools/inspect_game.py)
answers it without launching anything, read-only:

```sh
python3 tools/inspect_game.py "/path/to/Game/" \
    --our-library build/libEOSSDK-Linux-Shipping.so \
    --out inspection.json
```

It walks the game's binaries — native PE/ELF imports, delay-loads, .NET P/Invoke tables, even
`GetProcAddress`/`dlsym` string references — and reports, per EOS family:

- **LOADER-FATAL** — statically imported symbols we don't export. The game will not start.
- **fails at first call** — delay-loaded or dynamically resolved symbols we lack. The game
  starts, then breaks when it touches them.
- what it imports that we *do* cover, so you know how much of the game's surface is exercised.

Point `--reference-sdk` at Epic's original DLL to also cross-check against the real export
surface. The write-up of running this against the reference SDK is the
[export-surface census](../developers/internals/export-surface-census.qmd).

## `alpha_runner.py`: one safe, diagnostic game run

The runner automates the error-prone part of an alpha test: it finds the game's EOS SDK, runs the
import census, makes and verifies a recovery backup, stages the matching emulator artifact, creates a
run directory, launches the game without a shell, captures stdout/stderr, restores Epic's original
bytes, and emits a shareable bundle.

```sh
python3 tools/alpha_runner.py run "/path/to/Game" \
  --artifact build-win/EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll \
  -- "/path/to/Game/Game.exe"
```

The default profile and run area is `<game>/.eosr-alpha/`, which remains reachable when a launcher is
sandboxed (including Flatpak Steam). Override it with `--data-dir` when desired. Alpha runs default to
`full` tracing; use `--trace-level lifecycle` when measuring performance or reproducing a long session.

Steam/Proton often owns the real process lifetime. Use supervised manual mode in that case:

```sh
python3 tools/alpha_runner.py run "/path/to/Game" \
  --artifact build-win/EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll --manual
```

It prints the exact Steam launch options and waits. Launch and fully exit the game, then press Enter;
only then does it restore the original. If the runner or machine is killed while staged, recovery is
explicit and hash-checked:

```sh
python3 tools/alpha_runner.py restore --sdk "/path/to/Game/.../EOSSDK-Win64-Shipping.dll"
```

The local run directory keeps `runtime.json`, `launch.json`, `inspection.json`, `stdout.log`, and the
trace. Its sibling `*-bundle` directory is the one intended for sharing: it merges sanitized owned
metadata into `summary.json`, copies only complete structured trace records, and excludes stdout,
profile keys, display names, command arguments, and absolute paths.
